title: Security: threat model, review and drills
bridge: A failure drill is like a Playwright test for the platform's bad days. You start a run, break something on purpose, and assert what happens. Except it acts on the real platform, not a fake, so it never runs in CI, and Security watches it.
intro: The walls only work if they are in the right places and still hold after the build. This lesson covers the three security steps of G3. A threat model while we build, a design review of what we built, and drills that cause every failure on purpose.

picture.caption: Model the threats in week 4, check the built runtime in week 8, then break it on purpose with Security.

nodes.label: runtime as built: VMs, broker, proxy

steps.text: W4: walk the trifecta, list risks, owners, open decisions
every probe must fail and show in logs
each drill starts a drill ticket and breaks one thing
the VM dies; the platform must recover or stop and report
fixes, new tickets, and what each failure looks like
findings update the threat model; blockers get owners

sections.h: Find the gap in week 4, not after the pilot
p: A gap found in week 4 costs a ticket; after the pilot it costs trust. So Security looks at the runtime three times. The design while we build (G3-12). The built thing before the pilot (G3-40). Its failures, on purpose (G3-41, G3-42).

A threat model is a written list of what could go wrong, which wall stops it, and who owns it. Ronen from Security leads a half-day session. Sean and a DevOps engineer attend, with the G3 design and G0's gateway and GitHub App design as input.

sections.h: The lethal trifecta, part by part
p: The lethal trifecta (lesson p11-1) is untrusted input, outward actions and private data in one agent. With all three, an injected prompt can send private data out. The session walks it for every part of the runtime.

Untrusted input is everywhere: tickets, code, Slack, web pages. Outward actions exist: push, comment, post. So the third leg must be missing. Private data: none. Fake seed data only, no PHI, no staging or prod credentials, no Teleport, no VPN.

Then check each wall. No keys in the VM: a capability only, the token stays in the broker, no workflows permission. Egress: the Squid list, the DNS firewall, the S3 endpoint policy, the PrivateLink ports. Merging: the ruleset, exactly one approval, never the requester. And never apply, destroy, sync or workflow_dispatch.

callout.text: PHI never enters a prompt, and no key is ever in the VM. These are the walls the whole runtime is built around.

sections.h: Soft spots, decisions and the document
p: Some soft spots are known and must be named. The docker group is root on the VM. Push-triggered CI (cloud-ci, client-ci and sdk-ci run on push to any branch) runs an agent branch with CI's OIDC role and Vault. So G0's narrowing of the gha-runners Vault role must land before agents push.

Slack and Jira text are injection sources. The capability shows in the account's SSM command history. And inf's vault-store ClusterSecretStore reads all of kvv2, so the ai-agents namespace needs its own SecretStore and role.

The session decides four things. Is github.com on the proxy list? Is Nexus read access anonymous or a read-only user? Does the proxy get its own subnets, or does Squid run on inf behind PrivateLink? Is rootless Docker a Q1 item?
sections.because: We write every risk with its wall and owner, because a risk without an owner is a risk nobody fixes.

code.text:
# Threat model: agent runtime (G3-12, re-checked in G3-40)

| Risk | Wall or guidance | Owner | Ticket |
|---|---|---|---|
| Injected text makes Nova push our code to someone else's repo | Wall: github.com is off the proxy list; git goes through the broker, scoped to one repo | Platform | G3-07, G3-09 |
| Push-triggered CI runs an agent branch with CI's OIDC role and Vault | Wall: G0 narrows the gha-runners Vault role before agents push | DevOps | G0-11 |
| The docker group is root on the VM | Guidance now: the instance role is the real wall. Rootless Docker is a Q1 item | DevOps | decide |
| The capability shows in the account's SSM command history | Open: decide in the session | Security | G3-12 |

notes.text: Four columns: the risk, the wall or guidance against it, the owner, the ticket.
Why github.com stays off the proxy: an injected prompt could push our code to another repo with its own token.
A known soft spot with a wall that lives in another goal (G0).
Guidance, not a wall: written down so nobody thinks the docker group is safe.
An open decision gets an owner too.

sections.h: The design review: read, then probe
p: Designs drift while they are built. In week 8 Ronen reviews the runtime as built against the threat model. First he reads the deployed config. That is the sandbox instance role, security groups, the S3 endpoint policy, DNS firewall rules and PrivateLink allowed principals.

He also reads the broker scopes and the GitHub App's permissions: no workflows, no administration, no ruleset bypass. He checks G0 is in place. The gha-runners Vault role is narrowed, and CI on an agent branch cannot reach admin secrets.
Then come the probes: real attempts from a real sandbox, as user agent. Each must fail and show up in logs or alerts.
sections.because: We probe from inside a real sandbox, because a config can look right and still let something through.

code.file: probes for the G3-40 review (a sketch built from the ticket's list)
code.text:
# On a sandbox VM, as user agent, during the review. Every command must FAIL,
# and every failure must show up in logs or alerts.
curl -s -m 5 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/  # IMDS credentials
curl -s -m 5 -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://example.com                # a site not on the allow-list
dig +short not-on-the-list.example.org                                          # an unknown domain
git -C /work/fcp push origin HEAD:main                                          # push to main
git -C /work/fcp push origin HEAD:refs/heads/nova/RH-9999                       # another run's branch
# Then, with Security: another repo, another run's capability, another run's artifacts.

notes.text: Run as user agent, the user the harness runs as, on a real sandbox in the ai-agents account.
Read the instance's credentials from IMDS, the metadata service. Must fail.
A site that is not on the allow-list. Squid must refuse it, and the denial must reach VictoriaLogs.
An unknown domain must not resolve.
A push to main must be refused by the broker.
A push to a branch outside this run's scope must be refused too.
The last three probes need a second run and Security's help: another repo, another run's capability, another run's artifacts.

callout.text: Findings go into threat-model.md. Blockers become tickets with owners before week 9. The review ends in a sign-off or a short list of blockers for the pilot.

p: A playbook nobody tested is a guess. The drill kit has one script per failure, in ai-agents/drills/src/, one node:test file per area: vm.ts, agent.ts, outside-services.ts and people.ts. You run it with npm run drills -w drills.

Drills act on the real platform, so CI's npm test never runs them. Each drill starts a run on a drill ticket, with minute-scale timers. It checks the outcome through Temporal queries, Slack, Jira and logs.

VM faults use AWS FIS, the Fault Injection Service: terminate the VM mid-run, stop it, or send a Spot interruption. Agent faults use fixture tickets: a flaky-by-design test, a request to edit .github/workflows, a blocked site, a done with a failing check.

Service faults use drill-only switches: the gateway returns 529 for 20 minutes, the broker refuses Slack, the broker is scaled to 0. People drills: nobody approves, nobody answers, a person pushes to Nova's branch. Main moves with a conflict, one ticket comes twice, five at once, Stop.

sections.h: vm.ts, part 1: a VM killed mid-run
p: Here is the ticket's VM drill file, split in two. The first line, a path comment, is dropped. Drill is the kit's helper: one object with clients for Temporal, Slack, Jira, FIS and metrics.
sections.because: We assert on outcomes people care about, because a drill should prove the work survived, not that some function ran.

notes.text: The same assert and test as every node:test file (lesson p1-6).
Connect once, at the top of the file. Top-level await works in ES modules.
One minute in milliseconds, for readable deadlines.
Start a run on drill ticket DRILL-1 with a small frontend fix as the fixture.
Wait until Nova is working on a VM, and remember which VM.
Kill it with an AWS FIS experiment template, the way a real failure would.
Within 10 minutes, the run must be working again on a different VM (lesson g3-11).
The branch has a checkpoint: nothing was lost.
The dead-VM metric counted it, so the alert from lesson g3-15 would fire.
The dead VM no longer exists. It was released, never reused.

sections.h: vm.ts, part 2: two losses and a Spot warning
p: Part 2 has two more drills. The first checks the stop after two lost VMs. The second checks that a Spot warning pushes the work and retries on a fresh VM.
sections.because: We drill the second loss too, because the stop-and-report path runs rarely and would otherwise first run on a real ticket.

notes.text: A new drill ticket, so the drills never share state.
Twice: wait for a VM, then kill it.
Within 15 minutes the run must say Needs a person.
The thread's last message is the one runWithRecovery posts: "lost two VMs".
spot: true puts the run on a Spot VM, like a retryable routine.
Send a Spot interruption (FIS action aws:ec2:send-spot-instance-interruptions).
The harness checkpoints on the warning, and the run carries on on another VM.
The checkpoint is on the branch.

p: In G3-42 we run the whole kit with Ronen or a Security engineer, on the real platform, with drill tickets. The report goes under runs/drills/<date>/.
Small failures are fixed the same day. Anything bigger becomes a ticket with an owner. If it touches a wall, it blocks the pilot.

The goal's proof: /nova DRILL-100 in Slack, a plan, an approval, and a draft PR on the scratch repo. All from a fresh VM with no key inside. The probes confirm there was no key, and the blocked-site try is in VictoriaLogs. Last, add to the runbook what each failure looks like in Slack, Grafana and the logs.

callout.text: This is how we know G3 works before real pilot tickets arrive.

youNeed: paper or a text file for your answers

worked.do: Read vm.ts part 1, line 10. Which lesson's code must handle what this line causes, and which function?
worked.see: Lesson g3-11: workInSandbox throws SandboxDead, and runWithRecovery claims a fresh VM.

worked.do: Read line 11. Why does it wait for state Working with notVm set, and not for state Working alone?

worked.do: Read lines 12 to 14. For each assert, write which promise of the platform it checks.
worked.see: 12: nothing was lost (checkpoint). 13: the failure was counted (alerts work). 14: the dead VM is gone (never reused, no cost leak).

worked.do: Read part 2, lines 3 to 8. Which constant in recovery.ts makes this drill end where it does?
worked.see: MAX_LOST_VMS = 2. The second loss throws NeedsPerson after notify posts "lost two VMs".

worked.do: Read part 2, line 14. In which lesson does the harness react to a Spot warning, and what does it do?
worked.see: Lessons g3-8 and g3-11: spot-watch writes /run/nova/preempt; the harness checkpoints and exits preempted; the workflow retries on a fresh VM.

lab.faded: Plan the drill "a VM stopped mid-run" with the same shape as drill 1. Write the startTicket line with DRILL-4 and the FIS line with the stop action. The last step is yours: write the asserts. Say what the platform should do with a stopped VM that stops heartbeating.
lab.alone: Design a people drill for people.ts: "nobody approves the plan" on drill ticket DRILL-10, where waitForPerson runs in minutes. Write the steps and asserts as node:test lines. Say when the reminder must appear, when the run must end as parked, and what Jira must show. Use the timers from lesson g3-12.
lab.done: You can explain what every line of vm.ts proves, and your people drill checks both the reminder and the park.

quiz.q: In the lethal trifecta for our sandboxes, what is the private data?

options.text: None: fake seed data only, no PHI, no staging or prod credentials, no Teleport, no VPN.
options.why: With one leg missing, an injected prompt has nothing private to send out.

options.text: The fcp source code on the VM.
options.why: The code is ours but it is the work itself. The walls keep it from going to other repos.

options.text: The GitHub token the agent uses to push.
options.why: There is no token in the VM. The broker holds it; the VM has only a capability.

quiz.q: Why does CI's npm test never run the drills?

options.text: They are too slow for CI.
They act on the real platform: they start runs and terminate VMs.
options.why: That is why they run only with npm run drills -w drills, with drill tickets.

options.text: They need a Security engineer to approve each run.
options.why: Security joins the G3-42 session, but that is not why CI skips them.

quiz.q: Why must G0's narrowing of the gha-runners Vault role land before agents push?

options.text: Because the broker uses that Vault role to mint GitHub tokens.
options.why: The broker has its own secrets. This is about CI.

options.text: Because agents need Vault access to run tests.
options.why: Agents get no Vault access at all.

options.text: Because cloud-ci, client-ci and sdk-ci run on push to any branch, with CI's OIDC role and Vault.
options.why: An agent branch would otherwise run with secrets that reach admin.

words.plain: A written list of what could go wrong, the wall or guidance against it, and who owns it.
A known weak place in the design that is written down, with guidance or a later fix.
A real attempt to break a wall from inside a sandbox; it must fail and be logged.
A script that causes one failure on purpose during a test run and checks the outcome.
AWS Fault Injection Service: runs experiments that stop, terminate or interrupt real instances.
A Jira ticket in the drill project whose waits run in minutes instead of days.

tickets.why: This lesson explained the trifecta walk, the walls to check, the soft spots, the open decisions and the threat-model format.
walk: Book a half-day session in week 4. Ronen leads; Sean and a DevOps engineer attend. Bring the G3 design and G0's gateway and GitHub App design.
Walk the lethal trifecta for each part: untrusted input, outward actions, private data (none).
Check each wall: no keys in the VM, egress, merging, and never apply, destroy, sync or workflow_dispatch.
Name the soft spots: the docker group, push-triggered CI, Slack and Jira text, the SSM history, and inf's vault-store reading all kvv2.
Decide: github.com on the proxy list, Nexus read access, the proxy's subnets or Squid on inf, rootless Docker in Q1.
Write ai-agents/docs/threat-model.md with risk, wall or guidance, owner and ticket. Plan the re-check in week 8 (G3-40).

tickets.why: This lesson explained what the review reads in the deployed config and which probes must fail from a real sandbox.
walk: Read the deployed config with Ronen: instance role, security groups, S3 endpoint policy, DNS firewall rules, PrivateLink allowed principals.
Read the broker scopes and the GitHub App's permissions: no workflows, no administration, no ruleset bypass.
Run the probes from a sandbox as user agent (sketch above), plus another repo, another run's capability and another run's artifacts.
Check that every probe failed and shows up in logs or alerts.
Check G0 is in place: the gha-runners Vault role is narrowed, and push-triggered CI on an agent branch cannot reach admin secrets.
Update threat-model.md. Turn blockers into tickets with owners before week 9, and record the sign-off.

tickets.why: This lesson explained the drill kit's layout and the three VM drills line by line.
walk: Create the ai-agents/drills workspace with src/vm.ts (code above), agent.ts, outside-services.ts and people.ts, and a drills script. Keep it out of CI's npm test.
Write the Drill helper: startTicket, waitFor, fis, metric, branchHasCheckpoint, instanceExists, lastThreadMessage.
Ask for a drill Jira project and a scratch repo for drill PRs; ask Nave whether RhinoHealth/agent-scratchpads is meant for this.
Create AWS FIS experiment templates in the ai-agents account: terminate, stop, and send a Spot interruption. Add the orphan drill: a tagged VM with a fake run ID.
Add the agent fixtures: a flaky-by-design test, a request to edit .github/workflows, a blocked site, a done with a failing check.
Add drill-only switches for the gateway 529s, the broker refusing Slack and the broker scaled to 0.
Add the people drills: no approval, no answer, a push to Nova's branch. Then main moves with a conflict, one ticket twice, five at once, Stop.

tickets.why: This lesson explained how the drills run with Security, what happens to failures, and the end-to-end proof.
walk: Run npm run drills -w drills with Ronen or a Security engineer, on drill tickets. Keep the report under runs/drills/<date>/.
Fix small failures the same day. Make bigger ones tickets with owners. Anything that touches a wall blocks the pilot.
Prove the goal: /nova DRILL-100 in Slack, plan, approve, draft PR on the scratch repo.
Confirm with G3-40's probes that the VM held no key, and find the blocked-site try in VictoriaLogs.
Add to the runbook (G3-34) what each failure looks like in Slack, Grafana and the logs.

remember: Model the threats while you build, probe what you built, and break every part on purpose with Security.
